case_study_insert.main_stem: Wrenford Limestone Walling (WLW) is a partnership in the stone quarrying and building materials sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2004 by Tom Wrenford, the business extracts and dresses limestone walling stone for landscapers and builders and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WLW plans to invest $750,000 in a new diamond-wire cutting and dressing shed, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $375,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. WLW faces two operational problems: labour turnover among quarry operatives has reached 16% and a skills gap in diamond-wire sawing, alongside rising cutting waste.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Sales Report — Q3 2025: The dressing shed processed 18,500 units of walling stone at a breakage rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 17 to 9 per month. Market research of 300 architects and landscapers found that 68% specify natural limestone and 54% would pay up to $1.20 more per unit for certified low-carbon stone. Average delivery time is 5 days. Cutting waste is 9.0% of output, and on-the-job wire-saw certification for 12 of the 32 operatives would cost $600 per employee at the technical college.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Wrenford Limestone Walling for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.00% to 5.75%, the fourth rise this year, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Diesel and quarrying input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, and building-materials inflation is running at 6.8%, while heritage and landscaping construction spending grew 2.7% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WLW plans to expand with its new diamond-wire cutting and dressing shed. Explain two advantages for WLW of growing organically by opening the shed instead of taking over a rival quarry.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Organic expansion through the new dressing shed lets WLW grow at a pace its 32 workers and Tom Wrenford's democratic decision-making can absorb, keeping the flat structure and the culture that brought complaints down from 17 to 9 per month. A takeover of a rival quarry would fuse two workforces overnight, create clashes over pay and rostering, and risk losing the very operatives WLW needs to close its diamond-wire sawing skills gap — with turnover already at 16%, cultural disruption could prove expensive and slow.

Point 2: Organic growth avoids the premium price, lawyers' fees and hidden liabilities a takeover would carry, keeping the $750,000 investment within reach of a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. WLW also keeps full control over quality — the breakage rate already fell from 5.2% to 3.4% under its own supervision — whereas an acquired site would arrive with unknown stock, equipment and contracts, and weak integration could hit the certified low-carbon stone programme that 54% of surveyed architects and landscapers would pay $1.20 more per unit for.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wrenford Limestone Walling and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: WLW is launching its certified low-carbon walling stone. Consider print advertising in landscaping and architecture magazines, sponsoring a heritage-buildings exhibition, or social media marketing aimed at architects. Which should WLW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print advertising in landscaping and architecture magazines: Specialist print would place WLW's certified low-carbon stone in front of exactly the 68% of surveyed architects and landscapers who specify natural limestone, with technical credibility and a lasting physical copy. However, glossy space is expensive per enquiry, magazines circulate monthly rather than at the moment a buyer specifies stone, and response is hard to measure — risky for a partnership still funding a $750,000 shed with a bank loan.

Sponsoring a heritage-buildings exhibition: A single-day presence at a heritage and conservation exhibition would concentrate high-quality, decision-making buyers — conservation officers, heritage contractors and architects — and WLW could demonstrate dressed samples and cutting precision in person. The weaknesses are high one-off fees, limited attendance, and no reach beyond the event; the audience is narrow, and WLW also sells to everyday landscapers who never attend heritage shows.

Social media marketing aimed at architects: Architect-focused content (case studies, carbon figures, installation details) reaches the 54% willing to pay $1.20 more per unit for certified low-carbon stone at low cost, is measurable through enquiries and downloads, and can be sustained all year rather than on one exhibition day. It demands consistent quality content and may miss less digitally active small landscaping firms.

Recommendation: WLW should choose social media marketing aimed at architects. It reaches the exact premium-paying segment identified in research, costs least per qualified enquiry, and keeps the pipeline flowing beyond any single event — important while servicing the $450,000 loan. Print advertising is rejected as too slow and difficult to measure; the heritage exhibition is rejected as high-cost and narrowly attended, though a small stand could be a later addition once the certified range is fully launched.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WLW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WLW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: WLW's labour turnover among quarry operatives has reached 16%. Explain two benefits for WLW of using induction training for its new quarry operatives.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Induction training teaches new operatives site rules, the flat democratic reporting lines, and basic wire-saw safety before they touch the quarry face, sharply reducing the risk of injury on diamond-wire cutting equipment. For a workforce of only 32, one serious accident would remove a trained operative for months and disrupt the 18,500-unit quarterly processing target; induction also slows the churn feeding the 16% turnover because new starters feel supported rather than thrown onto the face to learn unsupervised.

Point 2: A structured induction sets quality expectations around breakage and waste from day one — explaining why 12 operatives lack wire-saw certification and why cutting waste is 9.0% of output. New recruits who understand the 3.4% breakage target and the certified low-carbon standard from the start make fewer costly mistakes, complement the $600 college certification route, and let democratic team meetings focus on improvement rather than re-teaching basics.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WLW's safety, turnover, waste and certification needs.

questions.question_text: WLW's breakage rate is 3.4%. Consider introducing quality control (inspection of finished stone) or quality assurance (prevention through process checks). Which should WLW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control (inspection of finished stone): Inspecting dressed walling units at the end of the shed would catch breakage and sub-standard cuts before they reach the 68% of buyers specifying natural limestone, protecting WLW's complaint count (already down from 17 to 9 per month) and its certified low-carbon reputation. It is relatively cheap and quick to start — hire or nominate an inspector, set tolerances, tick and reject. However, it detects defects after money has been spent cutting the stone, so waste and rework are already sunk costs, and it adds nothing to why breakage happens.

Quality assurance (prevention through process checks): Building quality checks into extraction, sawing, dressing and handling — blade maintenance schedules, moisture monitoring, verified low-carbon sourcing — attacks the causes of the 3.4% breakage rate and the 9.0% cutting waste at source. It raises consistency for the premium $1.20 certified range and cuts long-run costs, but requires training, documented procedures and cultural change, and benefits arrive slowly; the partnership must keep delivering 72,000 units a year while it is introduced.

Decision: WLW should choose quality assurance as its primary approach, supported by basic end-of-line inspection. With turnover at 16% and a skills gap in wire-sawing, fixing process discipline and operator competence is the only way to bring breakage sustainably below 3% and protect margins on the certified range; pure inspection is rejected because it accepts waste as inevitable and cannot differentiate WLW on carbon certification. Modest inspection remains as a safety net, but prevention must come first, backed by the $600 college certification for the 12 uncertified operatives.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to WLW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of WLW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of WLW with a well-justified decision covering waste, cost, certification and operator skills.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WLW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $375,000 ÷ ($18.00 − $10.50) = $375,000 ÷ $7.50 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.00 − $10.50 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WLW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. WLW's managers can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 72,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 22,000 units, to judge whether the dressing shed can be expanded further without undue risk.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.50 lets managers model the effect of a modest discount for volume landscaping customers, for example a 5% cut to $17.10 would drop contribution to $6.60, letting them judge whether extra volume would still cover the $375,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $375,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets needed to service the $450,000 bank loan, checking the new shed generates enough cash before committing any further capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($375,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $10.50 = $15.71 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, pinpoint the waste behind the 9.0% cutting loss, and decide whether to renegotiate the $10.50 variable cost with quarry suppliers amid the 8.4% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 22,000 units against 72,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $375,000 fixed costs; bank-loan feasibility for the $750,000 dressing shed; and unit-cost benchmarking at $15.71 to tackle 3.4% breakage and 9.0% cutting waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WLW's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has WLW's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $4,200,000 revenue − $2,310,000 cost of sales = $1,890,000; 2025 gross profit = $4,900,000 − $2,450,000 = $2,450,000. 2024 operating profit of $525,000 ÷ revenue of $4,200,000 = 12.5%; 2025 operating profit of $735,000 ÷ revenue of $4,900,000 = 15.0%. 2024 operating profit of $525,000 ÷ capital employed of $2,625,000 = 20.0%; 2025 operating profit of $735,000 ÷ capital employed of $3,500,000 = 21.0%. Revenue rose $700,000 while cost of sales rose just $140,000, so gross profit rose $560,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has improved, though returns on capital are rising only slowly. The move towards certified low-carbon stone lifted gross profit from $1,890,000 to $2,450,000 and the gross margin from 45.0% to 50.0% — clear evidence the $1.20 premium is sticking. Operating profit rose 40% to $735,000, but capital employed grew $875,000 to fund the dressing shed, so the return on capital edged up only one percentage point to 21.0%. Interest payable rose from $90,000 to $115,000. WLW must ensure the certified range volume grows enough to dilute that higher capital base, and the 8.4% diesel and quarrying input-cost rise threatens the 50.0% margin if not passed on through price rises.

Conclusion: WLW's profitability has improved. Gross profit, operating profit and absolute returns all rose, and gross margins widened strongly in 2025. The improvement is real but the return on capital gains are thin relative to the extra capital absorbed, so WLW should sweat the new shed hard — higher throughput, lower breakage and tight overhead control — before taking on further debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether WLW's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WLW of supplying certified low-carbon limestone walling stone instead of standard stone.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified low-carbon stone matches the 54% of 300 surveyed architects and landscapers willing to pay up to $1.20 more per unit, letting WLW charge a premium that protects its $7.50 contribution per unit even as diesel and quarrying input costs rise 8.4%. It also positions WLW for the growing heritage and low-carbon construction segment, strengthening specifications from the 68% of architects who already favour natural limestone and supporting the $750,000 dressing-shed business case.

Disadvantage: Certification demands audited sourcing, documented cutting waste below target and chain-of-custody paperwork — administration a 32-person partnership may struggle to resource. If the certified premium fails to hold in price-sensitive landscaping segments, WLW is left carrying higher compliance costs and tighter quality discipline (against a 3.4% breakage rate and 9.0% cutting waste) without extra revenue, squeezing margins and weakening the returns needed to service the $450,000 bank loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WLW's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.4% rise in diesel and quarrying input costs will affect WLW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): On WLW's $450,000 ten-year bank loan, a 0.75 percentage point rise adds roughly $3,400 a year in interest — modest against fixed costs of $375,000. Higher rates could also soften landscaping projects financed by clients, trimming order volumes, and raise the cost of any second-phase borrowing; WLW should seek a fixed-rate deal at renewal.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 per hour): Quarry operatives are WLW's largest cost block; most of the 32 staff are on or near the minimum wage. The increase adds about $0.81 an hour, roughly $1,690 per worker a year, or around $54,000 across the workforce — roughly 7% of current operating profit of $735,000. Democratic leadership and re-rostering could share the burden, but wage-driven turnover could accelerate, worsening the existing 16% rate.

Input cost inflation (8.4% diesel and quarrying costs): Diesel powers quarry plant and delivery; say fuel and consumables represent around 40% of the $10.50 variable cost ($4.20). An 8.4% rise adds about $0.35 per unit; at 72,000 units that is roughly $25,000–$30,000 a year. WLW can partially offset via the $1.20 certified premium, but passing on the full rise risks losing price-sensitive landscaping accounts.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It compounds across the entire workforce regardless of volume, adding roughly $54,000 a year — approaching a tenth of operating profit — and lands on top of a 16% turnover problem WLW is already trying to fix. The diesel rise (~$25,000–$30,000) is serious but controllable through price reviews, and the interest rise (~$3,400) is trivial; even so, WLW must combine premium pricing with retention policies and energy-efficient machinery to protect margins from all three.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WLW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WLW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WLW with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
